_meta.note: The event deck. Each entry is pure data: a set of multipliers on operating conditions, a duration, and how likely it is to come up. There is deliberately no bespoke code per event — adding one is a JSON entry.

effects.fuelPrice: multiplier on what fuel costs, on top of the spot price
effects.fare: multiplier on the fare that can be charged
effects.handlingCost: multiplier on airport and per-passenger costs
effects.completion: share of the schedule that operates at all
effects.loadCeiling: how full a carrier can fly a sector that is turning traffic away

_meta.design: Demand shocks glance off strong sectors, because a route already turning traffic away just spills less — see DECISIONS.md. So a demand event has to be severe to be felt at all, and most of the deck works through COST and COMPLETION instead, which bite regardless of how much spare demand a route has.
_meta.scope: Optional. `regions` limits an event to sectors touching those regions; `aircraftKlass` limits it to sectors flown by that class of aircraft.
_meta.historical: A timeline of real events on their real dates, fired only in the history scenario, layered on top of the random deck. eventId references a card in `events`; quarter is 1-4. sept11 and covid are the two cards with no generic equivalent.

events.name: Oil spike
events.blurb: Crude jumps on supply fears. Every departure costs more before a single seat is sold.

events.name: Oil glut
events.blurb: A supply glut sends crude down. Fuel is briefly cheap.

events.name: Pandemic scare
events.blurb: A health scare empties aircraft worldwide. Nobody is flying who does not have to.
events._comment: On the `health` axis with sars: a random pandemic scare must not open on top of a scripted outbreak, the same way an oil glut must not open during a spike. Free for present-day play, where this card is the only health card that can run and was already barred from re-drawing itself.

events.name: SARS outbreak
events.blurb: A respiratory outbreak empties cabins across Asia. Border screening and cancelled conferences do the rest; the rest of the world flies on.
events._comment: The 2003 historical beat, which used to fire the generic global `pandemic` card (demand 0.42 worldwide for its full 7 quarters). That is COVID-scale — the generic card is right as a random draw and wrong as SARS. Real SARS was regional and short: Asia-Pacific traffic collapsed for roughly two to three quarters while North Atlantic flying carried on. Scripted-only, like sept11 and covid: weight 0 and minTurn 999 keep it out of the random deck.

events.name: Recession
events.blurb: The economy turns. Corporate travel budgets go first, and fares follow.

events.name: Boom
events.blurb: A strong economy fills cabins and lets everyone charge more.

events.name: Pilot shortage
events.blurb: Crew are scarce and expensive, and the ones you have are being poached.

events.name: Air traffic control strike
events.blurb: Controllers walk out. A large slice of the schedule simply does not go.

events.name: Volcanic ash
events.blurb: Ash closes airspace. Nothing moves through the affected region.

events.name: Narrowbody grounding
events.blurb: A design fault grounds a whole class of aircraft. Regulators are in no hurry.

events.name: Widebody grounding
events.blurb: An engine problem grounds the widebody fleet while inspections run.

events.name: Airport charges rise
events.blurb: Operators push through a round of increases and there is nowhere else to land.

events.name: Airworthiness directive
events.blurb: A mandatory inspection program lands on the whole fleet at once.

events.name: Open-skies treaty
events.blurb: A liberalization deal opens traffic rights and the market grows.

events.name: Capacity discipline
events.blurb: The industry stops chasing share and fares firm across the board.

events.name: Tourism surge
events.blurb: A weak currency and a good summer fill every leisure route in the region.

events.name: Fare war
events.blurb: Somebody blinks first and the whole market follows the price down.

events.name: Severe winter
events.blurb: Weeks of de-icing, diversions and cancellations across the northern networks.

events.name: September 11
events.blurb: Terror attacks ground the system and empty the cabins. Fear and new security choke demand for months.

events.name: COVID-19 pandemic
events.blurb: A global pandemic closes borders and empties the skies. Nearly nobody is flying; only bailouts keep the industry alive.
events._comment: On the `health` axis with sars: a random pandemic scare must not open on top of a scripted outbreak, the same way an oil glut must not open during a spike. Free for present-day play, where this card is the only health card that can run and was already barred from re-drawing itself.

events.name: Market turmoil
events.blurb: Something has come loose in the wider economy. Nobody agrees yet on how bad it is, or on what exactly it will cost you.
events._comment: The chaos card. Its headline is constant and its bite is not: every effect is rolled fresh from a range each time it is drawn, so a player who has seen it once still does not know what this one costs. It is the only card in the deck that can land as a nuisance or as the worst quarter of a run, and it is deliberately wide on BOTH sides of 1 — sometimes the turmoil is other people's and traffic comes to you. Wide is the point; if it were tuned to a tight band it would just be another recession card.

events.name: Labour unrest
events.blurb: Contract talks have gone badly somewhere in the industry, and the mood is spreading. How far it goes is anyone's guess.
events._comment: The second ranged card, narrower and aimed at the cost line rather than the whole board. Two chaos cards rather than one so the deck cannot be read from a single draw — meeting turmoil once should not tell a player what the OTHER wildcard does.
